fit: All-Clad’s D3 12-inch fry pan is model 4112. The D5 12-inch polished fry pan is model SD55112. Both pages say stainless steel, a polished finish, oven and broiler safe up to 600 F, any stovetop including induction, hand washing, and a limited lifetime warranty.

Construction is the split. The D3 page says tri-ply construction that combines five metal layers into three functional layers. The D5 page says 5-ply bonded construction. The spec tables print Weight 3.000000 for the D3 and 4.000000 for the D5, and neither line names a unit.

sections.heading: All-Clad D3 vs D5 is a ply difference on the same 12-inch size
paragraphs: Both fry pans are titled 12 inch, and both spec tables say Size 12 inch, Material Stainless Steel, Exterior Finish Polished Stainless Steel, Made in United States, and Piece Count 1. Both detail blocks say the cookware is made in the USA with global components, bonded, engineered, and assembled in Canonsburg, Pennsylvania. Both say the handles are stainless and double-riveted, and both mention flared edges for pouring.

The D3 description says fully bonded tri-ply construction combining five metal layers into three functional layers: two stainless layers bonded to a three-layer aluminum and aluminum-alloy core. Read that sentence twice. It says three functional layers, and it also says five metal layers inside those three. The D5 description says 5-ply bonded construction, with alternating layers of aluminum and stainless steel, and calls D5 the premier range for even heating. A shopper who hears “five” on both pages is hearing two different sentences.

Oven and stovetop lines match. Both say oven and broiler safe up to 600 F, and both say extended heat over 500 F can change the color of the stainless without affecting performance. Both say high heat is for boiling, and that everyday cooking should start on low to moderate heat. Both say the pan works on any stovetop, including induction. Both say handwash only. The care blocks match closely: wash before first use, cool the pan before washing, and do not use oven cleaner, steel wool, or bleach.

sections.heading: The dimension lines do not describe the same footprint
paragraphs: The D3 12-inch spec table prints Dimensions 20.1 x 12.5 x 4.4 inches. That is the line on the D3 spec table. The D5 12-inch spec table prints Dimensions 15.0 x 8.6 x 2.9 inches. A pan whose title says 12 inch and whose dimension line says 8.6 inches across is not a line to trust without measuring. This table leaves dimensions off the shared rows for that reason. The D3 figure stays with the D3 notes under the fold.

Weight has a similar problem of a missing unit. The D3 table prints 3.000000. The D5 table prints 4.000000. All-Clad does not write lb, kg, or ounces next to those numbers on the pages opened here. A higher printed number is the D5 line. It is not, by itself, a finished weight you can put on a shelf drawing.

Both pages were in stock when opened. That can change. Match model 4112 or SD55112 on the box, then match 3-ply or 5-ply in the description. UPC on the D3 page is 011644502201. UPC on the D5 page is 011644010089.

sections.heading: How to choose, then what to confirm
paragraphs: Pick the D3 if you want model 4112, the 3-ply sentence, the 20.1 x 12.5 x 4.4 inch dimension line, and the weight number 3.000000. Pick the D5 if you want model SD55112, the 5-ply sentence, and the weight number 4.000000, and you have decided what to do about the 15.0 x 8.6 x 2.9 inch line on a 12-inch title.

Care is not a reason to pick one. Both tell you to preheat on low to moderate heat, dry food before it goes in, and let stainless release before you turn it. Both warn that salt in a cold pan can pit the inside, and that a hot pan should not go under cold water. The limited lifetime warranty covers All-Clad cookware on both pages. Read that warranty text on the pan you order. The D3 model page is the 12-inch fry pan already listed here, not a saucepan and not an 8-inch skillet.

faqs.q: Is All-Clad D5 the same metal stack as D3?
faqs.a: No. The D3 page says tri-ply construction that combines five metal layers into three functional layers. The D5 page says 5-ply bonded construction.

faqs.q: Are both 12-inch pans oven safe to the same temperature?
faqs.a: Yes. Both pages say oven and broiler safe up to 600 F, and both say heat over 500 F can discolor stainless without changing performance.

faqs.q: Can both go on induction?
faqs.a: Yes. Both pages say the pan is compatible with any stovetop, including induction.

faqs.q: Why are the dimension lines not in the table?
faqs.a: The D3 12-inch page prints 20.1 x 12.5 x 4.4 inches. The D5 12-inch page prints 15.0 x 8.6 x 2.9 inches. Those official lines do not describe the same footprint, so they are not set side by side as if they were.

faqs.q: What models and warranties are these?
faqs.a: D3 is model 4112. D5 is model SD55112. Both pages say a limited lifetime warranty, hand washing, and a polished stainless finish. The weight lines print 3.000000 and 4.000000 with no unit named.

title: Zojirushi vs Tiger: which to buy
description: The NS-ZCC10 is a 5.5-cup, 680 watt cooker made in Japan. The Tiger JBV-A10U is a 5.5-cup, 672 watt cooker made in China.
answer: Zojirushi lists the NS-ZCC10 at up to 5.5 cups (1.0 liter) and 680 watts, made in Japan.
Tiger lists the JBV-A10U as a 5.5-cup cooker, 1 liter and 672 watts, made in China.
The cabinets are close: 10-1/8 by 13 by 8-1/8 inches for Zojirushi, and 10.6 by 13.9 by 8.4 inches for the JBV-A10U.

verdict.heading: Choose the Zojirushi if
bullets: You want up to 5.5 cups at 680 watts, made in Japan.
You want the Neuro Fuzzy menu list, including sushi, sweet, semi-brown, and quick.
You have 8-1/8 inches of height and you want the 10-1/8 by 13 inch footprint.

verdict.heading: Choose the Tiger if
bullets: You want the 5.5-cup JBV-A10U at 672 watts.
You want synchro-cooking with the tacook plate and a 12-hour keep-warm line.
You want the cooker Tiger lists as made in China, at about 5.7 lb.

zojirushi-ns-zcc10.label: Menus
zojirushi-ns-zcc10.value: White, sushi, softer or harder, mixed, porridge, sweet, semi-brown, brown, rinse-free, quick

fit: The Zojirushi NS-ZCC10 is the 5.5-cup Neuro Fuzzy cooker: up to 5.5 cups or 1.0 liter, 10-1/8 by 13 by 8-1/8 inches, 120 volts and 680 watts, made in Japan. Tiger’s US kitchen list calls the JBV-A10U a 5.5-cup cooker. The JBV product spec table says 1 L (34 oz), 672 watts, 120 V, 60 Hz, and a cabinet of 10.6 by 13.9 by 8.4 inches.
Origin is the clean split on the spec tables: Japan for the NS-ZCC10, China for the JBV-A10U. Watts are close, 680 against 672. The menu lists are not the same length.

sections.heading: Zojirushi vs Tiger at the 5.5-cup size
paragraphs: These two are the same class of cooker: a 5.5-cup, about 1-liter microcomputer rice cooker, not an induction cooker and not a 10-cup pot. Zojirushi measures capacity in its own cup, about 6.1 fl oz or 180 mL, using raw short-grain white rice, and says other grains may vary. Tiger’s kitchen-products list puts JBV-A10U under Capacity 5.5 Cups, with dimensions that match the product spec table. The product table itself prints Capacity as 1 L and 34 oz, electric rating 672 W, and heating system Micom + Heating.

Footprints are close enough that a shelf which fits one may fit the other, and close enough that you should still measure. Zojirushi prints 10-1/8 by 13 by 8-1/8 inches. Tiger prints about 10.6 by 13.9 by 8.4 inches, and about 5.7 lb (2.6 kg). Zojirushi’s spec block on the store page does not print a weight. Tiger’s producing country is China. Zojirushi’s is Japan, and the store page says the cooker is cETLus listed.

A smaller Tiger is easy to confuse with this one. Tiger’s US homepage lists a Micom Rice Cooker JBS-A55U released on 21 April 2026. Tiger’s USA product page for the JBS-A55U says plain-rice capacity of 0.5 to 3 cups, 0.54 L, 360 watts, about 9.7 by 10.9 by 7.6 inches, and Japan as the producing country. That is a 3-cup cooker. It is not the JBV-A10U in this comparison.

sections.heading: Menus, keep warm, and what is in the box
paragraphs: Zojirushi’s menu line is the longer one: white rice on regular, sushi, softer, or harder, plus mixed, porridge, sweet, semi-brown, brown, rinse-free, and quick. The same page says automatic keep warm, extended keep warm, and a reheating cycle, a delay timer with two settings, a spherical inner pan, and a retractable power cord. It does not print a maximum keep-warm hour count in the block opened here.

Tiger’s JBV-A page names four menus: plain, brown, slow cooking, and synchro-cooking. It says keep warm for up to 12 hours. The included accessories are a tacook plate, a spatula, a rice measuring cup, and a recipe cookbook. Tiger says the plate cooks rice and a side dish together without the flavors mixing. The inner pot is described as aluminum with a fluorine coating. The warranty block says one year from the original purchase for Tiger electric products bought in the United States and Canada, for 120 V products.

Zojirushi’s store page links a limited warranty for electrical products and does not print the year count in the section opened here, so this table does not invent one. There is also an NS-ZCC18 on the same Zojirushi page, at up to 10 cups, 1.8 liters, and 1,000 watts. This comparison is the NS-ZCC10 only.

sections.heading: How to choose the 5.5-cup cooker
paragraphs: Pick the Zojirushi if you want 680 watts, made in Japan, the longer menu list, and a cabinet of 10-1/8 by 13 by 8-1/8 inches. Pick the Tiger JBV-A10U if you want 672 watts, the tacook plate, a stated 12-hour keep warm, and you accept China as the producing country on that spec table.

When the Zojirushi store page was opened, the NS-ZCC10 showed out of stock. Tiger’s kitchen list still presents the JBV-A series as a current cooker. Availability changes. Match NS-ZCC10, not NS-ZCC18, and match JBV-A10U, not JBV-A18U and not the 3-cup JBS-A55U. The worth-it note for the NS-ZCC10 uses these same Zojirushi figures.

faqs.q: Are the Zojirushi NS-ZCC10 and the Tiger JBV-A10U the same size?
faqs.a: Both are in the 5.5-cup class. Zojirushi says up to 5.5 cups or 1.0 liter. Tiger’s product table says 1 L (34 oz), and Tiger’s kitchen list calls the JBV-A10U a 5.5-cup cooker.

faqs.q: Which uses more watts?
faqs.a: Zojirushi lists 680 watts at 120 volts. Tiger lists 672 watts at 120 V and 60 Hz.

faqs.q: Where does each maker say the cooker is made?
faqs.a: Zojirushi says made in Japan. Tiger’s JBV-A10U spec table says the producing country is China. The newer JBS-A55U, a 3-cup cooker, is listed as made in Japan and is not this comparison.

faqs.q: What menus does each one name?
faqs.a: Zojirushi names white (regular, sushi, softer, or harder), mixed, porridge, sweet, semi-brown, brown, rinse-free, and quick. Tiger’s JBV-A page names plain, brown, slow cooking, and synchro-cooking, plus keep warm up to 12 hours.

faqs.q: Is the Tiger JBS-A55U the same cooker?
faqs.a: No. Tiger’s USA page for the JBS-A55U says 0.5 to 3 cups, 0.54 L, and 360 watts. The homepage dates that release to 21 April 2026. The 5.5-cup model in this comparison is the JBV-A10U.

title: Mr Heater Buddy vs Big Buddy: which to buy
description: The MH9BX is 4,000 or 9,000 BTU and up to 225 sq ft. The MH18B is 4,000, 9,000, or 18,000 BTU and up to 450 sq ft.
answer: The Portable Buddy MH9BX is 4,000 or 9,000 BTU and up to 225 sq ft, from one 1 lb propane cylinder.
The Big Buddy MH18B is 4,000, 9,000, or 18,000 BTU and up to 450 sq ft, from two 1 lb cylinders.
Both standard listings are marked indoor safe, with Massachusetts and Canada restrictions, and both have a tip-over shutoff and an oxygen depletion sensor.

verdict.heading: Choose the Buddy if
bullets: You want 4,000 or 9,000 BTU and up to 225 sq ft.
You want one 1 lb cylinder and a 3-hour run at the maximum setting.
You want the smaller heater, with a spec-table weight of 10.6 and no unit named.

verdict.heading: Choose the Big Buddy if
bullets: You want 18,000 BTU and up to 450 sq ft.
You can run two 1 lb cylinders, which the high setting needs.
You want hi, medium, and low, and you can tell the indoor listing from the Massachusetts and Canada version.

mr-heater-mh9bx.label: Indoor
mr-heater-mh9bx.value: Yes. Restricted in Massachusetts and Canada

specs.label: Indoor
specs.value: Yes on this listing. Restricted in Massachusetts and Canada

fit: Mr. Heater’s Portable Buddy page is model MH9BX: 4,000 or 9,000 BTU per hour, up to 225 sq ft, one 1 lb cylinder, hi and low, piezo ignition, an oxygen depletion sensor, and a tip-over shutoff. The spec table says 3 hours at the maximum BTU and 6 hours at the minimum.

The Big Buddy page is model MH18B: 4,000, 9,000, or 18,000 BTU, up to 450 sq ft, two 1 lb cylinders, and hi, med, and low. Both standard pages mark indoor safe as yes and list Massachusetts and Canada as restrictions. A separate Big Buddy page is the Massachusetts and Canada version, and that page marks indoor safe as no.

sections.heading: Mr Heater Buddy vs Big Buddy heat, area, and fuel
paragraphs: The Portable Buddy is the one-cylinder heater. Mr. Heater says it connects to a 1 lb cylinder, can connect to a 20 lb cylinder with an optional hose and filter, and has a swivel regulator and a fold-down handle. Heat is 4,000 or 9,000 BTU. The area line is up to 225 sq ft. The spec table also prints fuel use of 0.044 gallons per hour at 4,000 BTU and 0.099 gallons per hour at 9,000 BTU, a maximum elevation of 7000 ft, length 14.25, width 9, and height 15. Those length lines do not name inches. Weight prints as 10.6, also with no unit.

The Big Buddy is the two-cylinder heater. Heat is 4,000, 9,000, or 18,000 BTU. The area line is up to 450 sq ft. The spec table says the tank is two 1 lb propane cylinders, elevation 7,000 feet, weight 17.1, length 19, and width 12, again without naming the unit on the weight and the length. Ignition is piezo. The oxygen depletion sensor and the tip-over switch are yes. A hose and regulator are sold separately. Mr. Heater’s Buddy family notes say the 18,000 BTU high setting needs two 1 lb bottles, or a larger remote tank. One small bottle is not enough vapor for that high setting, and the tank can frost.

Warranty is a 3 year limited warranty on both spec tables. Thermostat optional is no on both. Fuel is propane on both. The use lists overlap: tents, campers, workshops, job sites, garages, patios, hunting blinds, ice-fishing shanties, and similar spots. The Big Buddy page also says cabins in the description.

sections.heading: Indoor-safe marks, and two different MH18B listings
paragraphs: The Portable Buddy page marks indoor safe as yes, and it lists state restrictions for Massachusetts and country restrictions for Canada. The standard Big Buddy page does the same: indoor safe yes, restricted in Massachusetts and Canada. Mr. Heater also sells a Big Buddy page titled as the Massachusetts and Canada version. That page says the heater is for recreational enclosures, construction sites, and outdoors, and its spec table marks indoor safe as no. If you are buying for Massachusetts or Canada, open that version and read the indoor-safe line before you treat the standard page as the one you can use there.

Run time is messier on the Portable Buddy page than the 3-hour line suggests. The spec table says 3 hours at maximum BTU and 6 hours at minimum BTU. A bullet on the same page says 225 sq ft of coverage for up to 5.4 hours. Those are both on the page. Use the table when you want the max-BTU and min-BTU pair, and do not ignore the 5.4-hour bullet. The Big Buddy spec table opened here does not print a run-time row. A bullet says 450 sq ft for up to 11 hours with dual tanks. There is no second official number next to it on that table.

Mr. Heater also says the fan has been removed on some Big Buddy MH18B units because of import tariffs, and that the Portable Buddy tip-over switch may now be audible when the heater is shaken. Those notes are on the product pages. A missing fan on one MH18B is not a different BTU rating. It is a reason to read the unit in front of you against the page.

sections.heading: How to choose, then what to confirm
paragraphs: Pick the Portable Buddy if you want 4,000 or 9,000 BTU, up to 225 sq ft, one 1 lb cylinder, and the 3-hour maximum run line in the spec table. Pick the Big Buddy if you want up to 18,000 BTU, up to 450 sq ft, and you can supply two 1 lb cylinders for the high setting. Both standard listings say indoor safe yes, with the Massachusetts and Canada restriction. The Massachusetts and Canada Big Buddy listing says indoor safe no.

Match MH9BX or MH18B on the heater, not the Buddy family name alone. Mr. Heater also sells a Little Buddy and a Hunting Buddy. This comparison is only MH9BX and MH18B. The space-heater safety guide is the place for the label checks and the official recall searches. It does not replace the BTU lines above. When these pages were opened, the Portable Buddy showed available and the standard Big Buddy showed out of stock. That can change.

faqs.q: How many BTU does each Buddy list?
faqs.a: The Portable Buddy MH9BX lists 4,000 or 9,000 BTU per hour. The Big Buddy MH18B lists 4,000, 9,000, or 18,000 BTU per hour.

faqs.q: How much area does Mr. Heater name?
faqs.a: Up to 225 sq ft for the MH9BX. Up to 450 sq ft for the MH18B.

faqs.q: How many propane cylinders does each one use?
faqs.a: The MH9BX runs on one 1 lb cylinder. The MH18B connects to two 1 lb cylinders. Mr. Heater’s Buddy notes say the 18,000 BTU setting needs both bottles, or a larger remote tank.

faqs.q: Are they marked indoor safe?
faqs.a: The standard MH9BX page and the standard MH18B page both mark indoor safe as yes, and both list Massachusetts and Canada restrictions. The separate Massachusetts and Canada MH18B page marks indoor safe as no.

faqs.q: What run time does the Portable Buddy table print?
faqs.a: 3 hours at the maximum BTU and 6 hours at the minimum. A bullet on the same page also says up to 5.4 hours. The Big Buddy table does not print a run-time row. A bullet there says up to 11 hours with dual tanks.
